title: Matrix Algebra
intro: Matrices, determinants, rank, inverses, linear systems and eigenvalues, step by step.

sec.s: A matrix is a rectangular arrangement of numbers or other mathematical entries written in rows and columns.

b.x: A matrix is a rectangular arrangement of numbers or other mathematical entries written in rows and columns. Matrices provide a compact way to represent data, linear equations, transformations, and relationships among variables.
Examples of where matrices are used

x: Computer graphics: rotating, scaling, and moving images.
Machine learning: storing datasets, model weights, and batches of numerical data.
Computer networks: representing connections between computers.
Economics: describing input-output relationships among industries.
Statistics: storing observations and calculating covariance.
Engineering: analysing electrical circuits and mechanical systems.
Cryptography: some encryption methods use matrix operations.
Solving simultaneous linear equations: several equations can be represented by one matrix equation.

sec.s: Pitfalls to avoid

x: Adding matrices of different orders. Addition requires the same order.
Multiplying matrices without checking inner dimensions.
Assuming AB = BA. Matrix multiplication is generally not commutative.
Confusing Aᵀ with A⁻¹. They are equal only for an orthogonal matrix.
Calculating a determinant for a non-square matrix. Determinants are defined only for square matrices.
Forgetting the negative sign in the 2 x 2 determinant ad - bc.
Using the wrong +, -, + cofactor sign pattern in a 3 x 3 determinant expansion.
Trying to invert a matrix with determinant zero.
Treating rank as the number of rows without checking independence.
Forgetting to apply row operations to the constants column in an augmented matrix.
Claiming that det(A) = 0 always means no solution. It can mean no solution or infinitely many solutions.
Treating the zero vector as an eigenvector. Eigenvectors must be non-zero.
Solving det(A - λ I) = 0 but forgetting to solve (A - λ I)v = 0 for eigenvectors.
In Cayley-Hamilton, replacing the constant term by a scalar number rather than that number times I.
Multiplying an equation by A⁻¹ before establishing that A is invertible.

sec.s: Revision checklist

x: A matrix is a rectangular arrangement of entries; its order is rows x columns.
Addition and subtraction require equal orders.
Matrix multiplication requires matching inner dimensions and is generally not commutative.
The transpose interchanges rows and columns.
Determinants are defined for square matrices and help identify invertibility.
A square matrix is invertible exactly when its determinant is non-zero.
Skew-symmetric matrices satisfy Aᵀ = -A and have zero diagonal entries over the real numbers.
Orthogonal matrices satisfy Aᵀ A = I and have inverse Aᵀ.
Rank measures the number of linearly independent rows or columns.
For AX = B, an invertible A gives the unique solution X = A⁻¹B.
The rank criterion determines whether a linear system is consistent and whether it has a unique solution.
Eigenvectors satisfy Av = λ v and must be non-zero.
The Cayley-Hamilton theorem says a square matrix satisfies its own characteristic polynomial.
The theorem can reduce high powers and help calculate the inverse of an invertible matrix.
